claim: Witnessing another person's suffering elicits vicarious brain activity in areas that are active when we ourselves are in pain.
source: Witnessing another person's suffering elicits vicarious brain activity in areas that are active when we ourselves are in pain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract, drawing from the broader literature on empathy and pain observation.

claim: Participants donate more money on trials in which the confederate expressed more pain.
source: Participants donate more money on trials in which the confederate expressed more pain.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Activity of the somatosensory cortex I (SI) hand region explains variance in donation.
source: Electroencephalography shows that activity of the somatosensory cortex I (SI) hand region explains variance in donation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the EEG experiment reported in the abstract and results section.

claim: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) altering SI activity interferes with the pain–donation coupling only when pain is expressed by the hand.
source: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) shows that altering this activity interferes with the pain–donation coupling only when pain is expressed by the hand.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the TMS experiment reported in the abstract and results section.

claim: High-definition transcranial direct current stimulation (HD-tDCS) altering SI activity interferes with pain perception.
source: High-definition transcranial direct current stimulation (HD-tDCS) shows that altering SI activity also interferes with pain perception.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the HD-tDCS experiment reported in the abstract and results section.

claim: Vicarious somatosensory activations contribute to prosocial decision-making.
source: These experiments show that vicarious somatosensory activations contribute to prosocial decision-making and suggest that they do so by helping to transform observed reactions of affected body-parts into accurate perceptions of pain that are necessary for decision-making.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Vicarious somatosensory activations help transform observed reactions of affected body-parts into accurate perceptions of pain necessary for decision-making.
source: These experiments show that vicarious somatosensory activations contribute to prosocial decision-making and suggest that they do so by helping to transform observed reactions of affected body-parts into accurate perceptions of pain that are necessary for decision-making.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation inferred from the combined experimental findings.

claim: People are more likely to engage in prosocial behaviour when they feel empathy for the person in distress.
source: Some researchers have shown that people are more likely to engage in prosocial behaviour when they feel empathy for the person in distress (Batson, 1981) and that self-reported emphatic concern is related to prosocial behaviour (FeldmanHall et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Self-reported empathic concern is related to prosocial behaviour.
source: Some researchers have shown that people are more likely to engage in prosocial behaviour when they feel empathy for the person in distress (Batson, 1981) and that self-reported emphatic concern is related to prosocial behaviour (FeldmanHall et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to FeldmanHall et al., 2015.

claim: Empathy is a poor predictor of prosociality.
source: Others have shown that empathy is a poor predictor of prosociality (Vachon et al., 2014; Jordan et al., 2016), with prosocial decisions often driven by other motives (e.g. status; Bloom, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Prosocial decisions are often driven by motives other than empathy, such as status.
source: Others have shown that empathy is a poor predictor of prosociality (Vachon et al., 2014; Jordan et al., 2016), with prosocial decisions often driven by other motives (e.g. status; Bloom, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bloom, 2017.

claim: Experiments that specifically manipulate brain activity in empathy-related regions and measure prosociality are missing.
source: Unfortunately, experiments that specifically manipulate brain activity in empathy-related regions and that measure prosociality are missing, limiting our neuroscientific understanding of whether and how empathy is mechanistically linked to prosociality (Keysers and Gazzola, 2017; Zaki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Witnessing somebody in pain activates two networks, depending on the nature of the stimulus.
source: Witnessing somebody in pain activates two networks, depending on the nature of the stimulus (Keysers et al., 2010; Lamm et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: If the pain of the other is deduced from abstract symbols or facial expressions alone, a network involving the anterior insula (AI) and the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) is activated.
source: If the pain of the other is deduced from abstract symbols or facial expressions alone, a network involving the anterior insula (AI) and the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) is activated.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the literature on pain observation.

claim: AI and ACC activity correlates with personal distress.
source: The AI and ACC activity correlates with personal distress (Singer et al., 2004), perceived unpleasantness (Rainville et al., 1997) and perceived pain intensity (Lamm et al., 2011), and is therefore thought to code for the unpleasantness of the pain of the other (Lamm et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Singer et al., 2004.

claim: AI and ACC activity correlates with perceived unpleasantness.
source: The AI and ACC activity correlates with personal distress (Singer et al., 2004), perceived unpleasantness (Rainville et al., 1997) and perceived pain intensity (Lamm et al., 2011), and is therefore thought to code for the unpleasantness of the pain of the other (Lamm et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rainville et al., 1997.

claim: AI and ACC activity correlates with perceived pain intensity.
source: The AI and ACC activity correlates with personal distress (Singer et al., 2004), perceived unpleasantness (Rainville et al., 1997) and perceived pain intensity (Lamm et al., 2011), and is therefore thought to code for the unpleasantness of the pain of the other (Lamm et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lamm et al., 2011.

claim: AI and ACC activity is thought to code for the unpleasantness of the pain of the other.
source: The AI and ACC activity correlates with personal distress (Singer et al., 2004), perceived unpleasantness (Rainville et al., 1997) and perceived pain intensity (Lamm et al., 2011), and is therefore thought to code for the unpleasantness of the pain of the other (Lamm et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the cited correlational findings.

claim: If the injured body part is visible and in the focus of attention, the somatosensory cortices (SI and SII) are also recruited.
source: If the injured body part is visible and in the focus of attention, the somatosensory cortices (SI and SII) are also recruited (Bufalari et al., 2007; Cheng et al., 2008; Keysers and Gazzola, 2009; Lamm et al., 2011; Nummenmaa et al., 2012; Morrison et al., 2013; Ashar et al., 2017; Christov-Moore and Iacoboni, 2016) and consequently included in the network of regions participating in human empathy (Keysers et al., 2010; de Waal and Preston, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The affective and somatosensory networks are also active when experiencing pain.
source: The affective and somatosensory networks are also active when experiencing pain (Melzack, 2001; Iannetti and Mouraux, 2010; Lockwood et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Vicarious activation while witnessing the pain of others is interpreted as the neural correlate of emotional contagion.
source: Because of that, many interpret vicarious activation while witnessing the pain of others as the neural correlate of emotional contagion, feeling vicariously what we see someone else experience, a core component of empathy (Koban et al., 2013; Corradi-Dell'Acqua et al., 2011; Jackson et al., 2006; Lamm et al., 2011; Cui et al., 2015; Singer et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an interpretation from the literature, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The emotional states of others are understood through personal, embodied representations.
source: In this perspective, the emotional states of others are understood through personal, embodied representations that allow empathy and accuracy in perceiving other emotions to increase on the basis of the observer's past experiences (Preston and de Waal, 2002; de Waal and Preston, 2017).
evidence: This is a theoretical perspective supported by citations.

claim: Pharmacological studies provide causal evidence for the involvement of our own experience of pain, via the insula and anterior cingulate cortex, in perceiving the pain of other individuals.
source: Pharmacological studies provide causal evidence for the involvement of our own experience of pain, via the insula and anterior cingulate cortex, in perceiving the pain of other individuals (Rütgen et al., 2015, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to pharmacological studies.

claim: The opioidergic circuit might code representations of aversive outcomes that are derived through both direct and indirect experiences.
source: This evidence pin-points to the opioidergic circuit, which might code representations of aversive outcomes that are derived through both direct and indirect experiences (Haaker et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on cited evidence.

claim: The pain vicariously felt because of the recruitment of pain-related regions while viewing the pain of others is thought to motivate prosocial behavior.
source: Much like the original proposal of Adam Smith (Smith, 1759), the pain vicariously felt because of the recruitment of these pain-related regions while viewing the pain of others is then thought to motivate prosocial behavior, which then simply serves to reduce the vicariously felt pain (Batson, 1981; Hein et al., 2010, 2016; Ma et al., 2011; Tomova et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by multiple citations.

claim: Testing the causal contribution of mapping the pain of others onto our own pain representations in social decision-making has remained poorly explored in neuroscience.
source: Testing the causal contribution of mapping the pain of others onto our own pain representations in social decision-making has remained poorly explored in neuroscience because most scientists focus on the affective network (AI, ACC), which lies too deep in the brain to allow its selective targeting with traditional non-invasive neuro-manipulation tools (Keysers and Gazzola, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature, supported by citation.

claim: The affective network (AI, ACC) lies too deep in the brain to allow its selective targeting with traditional non-invasive neuro-manipulation tools.
source: Testing the causal contribution of mapping the pain of others onto our own pain representations in social decision-making has remained poorly explored in neuroscience because most scientists focus on the affective network (AI, ACC), which lies too deep in the brain to allow its selective targeting with traditional non-invasive neuro-manipulation tools (Keysers and Gazzola, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a technical limitation, supported by citation.

claim: The hand representation of SI is superficial and reachable with TMS.
source: Here, we leverage the less investigated hand representation of SI, which is superficial and reachable with TMS, to address two questions: does activity in the somatosensory cortex (measured using EEG) explain prosocial behavior on a trial-by-trial basis and does disturbing (with TMS) this activity alter decision-making?
evidence: This is stated as a methodological rationale based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: Ventral regions of SI have been reported to be involved in emotional facial perception.
source: In addition, ventral regions of SI have been reported to be involved in emotional facial perception (e.g Adolphs et al., 2000; van der Gaag et al., 2007; Preston and de Waal, 2002; but see Rütgen et al., 2015 for absence of SI activity in the perception of facial expression of pain).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations, with a note about contradictory evidence.

claim: Participants donated on average the same amount in the Face and Hand conditions.
source: Participants (Table 1) donated on average the same amount in the Face and Hand conditions (Face: M = 2.14€, SD = 1.2; Hand: M = 2.16€, SD = 1.2; dependent sample t-test t(28)=–0.2, p=0.8)
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: There was more variability in donation for the Face condition compared to the Hand condition.
source: but comparing the standard deviation in donation within each participant showed more variability in donation for the Face condition (Face: MSD = 1.47, SDSD = 0.44; Hand: MSD = 1.22, SDSD = 0.40; dependent sample t-test t(28)=4, p=0.0004).
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Participants' donation was driven by the intensity of the reaction shown in the InputMovie.
source: To assess whether participants' donation was driven by the intensity of the reaction shown in the InputMovie, for each participant, we performed a robust linear regression (Holland and Welsch, 1977) between the intensity attributed to the movies by an independent pool of participants and the Z-donation. The analysis confirmed that participants' Z-donation closely followed the pain intensity shown in the InputMovies (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG experiment supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the Face condition, all participants had regression slopes that were positive and significantly different from zero.
source: In the Face condition, all participants had regression slopes that were positive and significantly different from zero (Face slope: M = 0.48, SD = 0.6, average t value for Face slope = 21.9, SD = 17, all p<0.05; group one-sample t-test on Face slopes t(28) = 37.9 p=0.0006E-21).
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: In the Hand condition, most participants showed positive and significant slopes between movie intensity and donation.
source: In the Hand condition, one participant had a negative slope but the regression was not significant (t = −0.17, p=0.8), a second participant had a positive but not significant slope (t = 1.89, p=0.06), whereas the remaining participants all showed positive and significant slopes (all p<0.05).
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The average slope did not differ between the Face and Hand conditions.
source: Importantly, the average slope did not differ between the two conditions (paired t-test t(28)=–1 p=0.3).
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: A dorsal somatosensory cluster (dSI-L) was identified at MNI coordinates (x,y,z) = −30,–36, 62.
source: We then identified voxels in the left SI where the BOLD signal correlated with reported painfulness (see 'Supplementary information, Pain localizer experiment'), and used the following clusters as ROIs for the EEG beam-forming analysis: a dorsal (dSI-L; peak at MNI(x,y,z) = −30,–36, 62) and a ventral (vSI-L; peak at MNI(x,y,z,) = −54,–19, 32) somatosensory cluster (Figure 2B; Maldjian et al., 1999; Mancini et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI pain localizer experiment, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A ventral somatosensory cluster (vSI-L) was identified at MNI coordinates (x,y,z) = −54,–19, 32.
source: We then identified voxels in the left SI where the BOLD signal correlated with reported painfulness (see 'Supplementary information, Pain localizer experiment'), and used the following clusters as ROIs for the EEG beam-forming analysis: a dorsal (dSI-L; peak at MNI(x,y,z) = −30,–36, 62) and a ventral (vSI-L; peak at MNI(x,y,z,) = −54,–19, 32) somatosensory cluster (Figure 2B; Maldjian et al., 1999; Mancini et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI pain localizer experiment, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Variation in activity in dSI-L explained variation of Z-donation in the Hand condition in the time windows between 420 and 452 ms.
source: Results show that variation in activity in dSI-L explained variation of Z-donation in the Hand condition in the time windows between 420 and 452 ms (cluster-statistic = 142.2, p=0.002) and between 458 and 476 ms (cluster-statistic = 91.4 ms, p=0.006) after the belt hits the confederate's hand.
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Variation in activity in dSI-L explained variation of Z-donation in the Hand condition in the time windows between 458 and 476 ms.
source: Results show that variation in activity in dSI-L explained variation of Z-donation in the Hand condition in the time windows between 420 and 452 ms (cluster-statistic = 142.2, p=0.002) and between 458 and 476 ms (cluster-statistic = 91.4 ms, p=0.006) after the belt hits the confederate's hand.
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Activity in dSI-L related to Z-donation in Face condition between 516 and 602 ms.
source: Activity in dSI-L also related to Z-donation in Face condition but later in time, between 516 and 602 ms (cluster-statistic = 602.5 ms, p=0.0009), between 608 and 754 ms (cluster-statistic = 333.8 ms, p=0.0009), and also between 808 and 880 ms (cluster-statistic = 330 ms, p=0.0009) after the noxious stimulation was delivered.
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Activity in dSI-L related to Z-donation in Face condition between 608 and 754 ms.
source: Activity in dSI-L also related to Z-donation in Face condition but later in time, between 516 and 602 ms (cluster-statistic = 602.5 ms, p=0.0009), between 608 and 754 ms (cluster-statistic = 333.8 ms, p=0.0009), and also between 808 and 880 ms (cluster-statistic = 330 ms, p=0.0009) after the noxious stimulation was delivered.
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Activity in dSI-L related to Z-donation in Face condition between 808 and 880 ms.
source: Activity in dSI-L also related to Z-donation in Face condition but later in time, between 516 and 602 ms (cluster-statistic = 602.5 ms, p=0.0009), between 608 and 754 ms (cluster-statistic = 333.8 ms, p=0.0009), and also between 808 and 880 ms (cluster-statistic = 330 ms, p=0.0009) after the noxious stimulation was delivered.
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: vSI-L brain activity explained Z-donation only in the Face condition in the time window between 402 and 430 ms.
source: vSI-L brain activity explained Z-donation but only in the Face condition in the time window between 402 and 430 ms (cluster-statistic = 102 ms, p=0.005; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG experiment supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Participants varied their donations from trial-to-trial more in the Face than in the Hand condition in the TMS experiment.
source: The within-subject ANOVA with two factors, Condition (Face and Hand) and TMS (Active and Sham), on the standard deviation calculated across the donation of each participant reveals that participants varied their donations from trial-to-trial more in the Face than in the Hand condition (main effect of condition F(1,14) = 98, p=0.001E–4)
evidence: This is a finding from the TMS experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: TMS had no effect on the average Z-donation in either task.
source: TMS had no effect on the average Z-donation in either task, as indicated by the repeated ANOVA with factor Condition (Face and Hand) and TMS (Active and Sham): TMS F(1,14) = 2.3, p=0.15, TMS x Condition F(1,14) = 0.5, p=0.56.
evidence: This is a finding from the TMS experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The slopes for the Face condition are steeper than those for the Hand condition in the TMS experiment.
source: The analysis showed that the slopes for the Face condition are steeper than those for the Hand (Face: M = 0.56, SD = 0.06; Hand: M = 0.49, SD = 0.14; Main effect of Condition: F(1,14) = 7, p=0.02).
evidence: This is a finding from the TMS experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: TMS showed a significant interaction effect between Condition and TMS on the slope between movie intensity and donation.
source: Interestingly, the ANOVA showed a significant interaction effect (F(1,14) = 4.8, p=0.04, partial η²=0.25; Figure 2C) with a larger TMS effect in the Hand compared to that in the Face condition.
evidence: This is a finding from the TMS experiment supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Active rTMS on SI significantly flattened the relationship between intensity and donation only for the Hand condition.
source: A Newman-Keuls post-hoc test indicated that active rTMS on SI significantly flattened the relationship between intensity and donation only for the Hand condition (Hand Sham M = 0.54, DS = 0.1; Hand TMS M = 0.45, DS = 0.2; p=0.02).
evidence: This is a finding from the TMS experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: There is no evidence for a TMS effect on the slope in the Face condition.
source: There is no evidence for such an effect in the Face condition (Face Sham M = 0.55, SD = 0.06; Face TMS M = 0.56, SD = 0.06; p=0.6).
evidence: This is a finding from the TMS experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The null hypothesis of no sizable effect of TMS in the Face condition is 5.7 times more likely than the alternative hypothesis.
source: We then performed a Bayesian one sample t-test using JASP with default priors (https://jasp-stats.org) that showed that the null hypothesis is 5.7 times more likely than the alternative H1 (Bayes factor p[H0:index ≥0|data]/p[H1:index <0|data]=5.7), providing positive evidence for the absence of a sizable effect in the Face condition (Kass and Raftery, 1995).
evidence: This is a finding from the TMS experiment supported by Bayesian statistical analysis.

claim: The TMS effect on the Hand condition did not correlate with any of the TMS side effects perceived by the participant.
source: The effect on the Hand condition did not correlate with any of the TMS side effects perceived by the participant while performing the experiment (measured by questionnaire, all p>0.05).
evidence: This is a finding from the TMS experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: TMS on the SI hand representation interferes with the process that normally couples a person's donation to the needs of the other person when this need is perceived through the movements of the affected body part.
source: This suggests that TMS on the SI hand representation interferes with the process that normally couples a person's donation to the needs of the other person (i.e. the observed pain intensity) when this need is perceived through the movements of the affected body part (Hand condition), but this is less the case when the need is perceived through facial expressions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the TMS experimental findings.

claim: Participants did not use the rating scale differently in the three conditions (Face, Hand, Color) in the HD-tDCS experiment.
source: A 2 Stimulation (tDCS and Sham) x 3 Condition (Face, Hand and Color) repeated measures ANOVA on the standard deviation calculated for the participants' rating reveals that participants did not use the rating scale differently in the three conditions (main effect of condition F(1,24) = 0.4, p=0.5)
evidence: This is a finding from the HD-tDCS experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Average rating remained stable across conditions in the HD-tDCS experiment.
source: A Stimulation (tDCS and Sham) x Condition (Face, Hand and Color) ANOVA on the average rating revealed that average rating remained stable across conditions (Stimulation F(1,24) = 0.5, p=0.5; Condition F(1,48) = 0.8, p=0.5; Interaction F(1,48) = 0.3, p=0.7).
evidence: This is a finding from the HD-tDCS experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The correlation coefficients between movie intensity and rating differed between conditions in the HD-tDCS experiment.
source: The analysis showed that the correlation coefficients differed between conditions (Face: M = 1.3, SD = 0.2; Hand: M = 1, SD = 0.2; Color: M = 1.2, SD = 0.3; Main effect of Condition: F(2,48) = 17, p<0.002E–3).
evidence: This is a finding from the HD-tDCS experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The Hand condition had a lower correlation coefficient than both the Face and Color conditions in the HD-tDCS experiment.
source: A post-Hoc Newman-Keuls test revealed that the Hand condition had a lower correlation coefficient than both the Face and Color conditions, while the latter did not differ from each other.
evidence: This is a finding from the HD-tDCS experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: tDCS had a different effect depending on the conditions (Face, Hand, Color).
source: Interestingly, tDCS had a different effect depending on the conditions (Interaction: F(2,48) = 3.4, p=0.04, η²=0.12).
evidence: This is a finding from the HD-tDCS experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: tDCS on SI significantly improved the relationship between intensity and rating for the Hand condition.
source: Planned paired t-test comparison between sham and tDCS session for each condition indicated that the tDCS on SI significantly improved the relationship between intensity and rating for the Hand condition (Hand Sham: M = 1, DS = 0.2; Hand tDCS: M = 1.1, DS = 0.2, t(24) = –2, p=0.04)
evidence: This is a finding from the HD-tDCS experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: tDCS showed a trend for reduction in the relationship between intensity and rating in the Face condition.
source: while it showed a trend for reduction in the Face condition (Face Sham: M = 1.3, DS = 0.2; Face tDCS: M = 1.2, DS = 0.2; t(24) = 1.8 p=0.07)
evidence: This is a finding from the HD-tDCS experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: tDCS showed no appreciable change in the Color condition.
source: and no appreciable change in the Color condition (Color Sham: M = 1.3, DS = 0.2; Color tDCS: M = 1.2, DS = 0.3; t(24) = 1, p=0.3).
evidence: This is a finding from the HD-tDCS experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The null hypothesis for the Color condition in the HD-tDCS experiment was 3.1 times more likely than the alternative hypothesis.
source: The Bayes factor indicated that the H0 was 3.1 times more likely than the H1, confirming that the Color condition does not change after HD-tDCS.
evidence: This is a finding from the HD-tDCS experiment supported by Bayesian statistical analysis.

claim: The Hand and Face effects in the HD-tDCS experiment did not correlate with any of the tDCS side effects perceived by participants.
source: The Hand and Face effects did not correlate with any of the tDCS side effects perceived by participants while performing the experiment (all p>0.05).
evidence: This is a finding from the HD-tDCS experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The timing of SI activity followed the timing of the information in the movies.
source: Figure 3 shows how the timing of that activity followed the timing of the information in the movies: the hand immediately retracts at the moment the belt hits the hand, and SI activity had a sharp and sudden peak in explanatory power, whereas the facial expression develops more slowly after the shock is delivered, and SI activity showed a more progressive and sustained explanatory power.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EEG data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The ventral and dorsal sector of the functionally localized SI nociceptive representation behave differently in the task.
source: Figure 3 also shows that the ventral and dorsal sector of our functionally localized SI nociceptive representation behave differently in our task, with the dorsal (hand) ROI explaining donation for either source of information (Face or Hand) and the ventral (face) ROI being explanatory only for facial expressions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EEG data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Only 10% of neurons involved in performing an action become recruited while observing that action.
source: decades of work on mirror neurons for actions show that only 10% of neurons involved in performing an action become recruited while observing that action (Gallese et al., 1996; Keysers et al., 2003; Mukamel et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to mirror neuron research.

claim: SI activity significantly predicted the donation only during the second half of the Hand movie, in which the victim's hand is compressed by the belt and reacts to it.
source: Interestingly, SI activity significantly predicted the donation only during the second half, in which the victim's hand is compressed by the belt and reacts to it.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EEG experimental findings.

claim: SI's ability to represent the impact of the belt on the hand or the reaction of the victim to the stimulation on the hand induced the prosocial decision-making.
source: This suggests that it is SI's ability to represent the impact of the belt on the hand or the reaction of the victim to the stimulation on the hand that induced the prosocial decision-making.
evidence: This is an interpretation inferred from the EEG findings.

claim: SI activation in the hand region contributes to prosocial decision-making by transforming the sight of hand-movements caused by a swat into a perception of pain-intensity.
source: Our results suggest that SI activation in the hand region contributes to prosocial decision-making by transforming the sight of hand-movements caused by a swat into a perception of pain-intensity, which then serves as an input to a decision-making process elsewhere.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation inferred from the combined experimental findings.

claim: If trial-by-trial perception is perturbed, the decision to help no longer optimally follows the trial-by-trial variance in pain experienced by others.
source: If this trial-by-trial perception is perturbed, our decision to help no longer optimally follows the trial-by-trial variance in pain experienced by others.
evidence: This is an interpretation inferred from the TMS experimental findings.

claim: Disturbing the activity of the SI hand region with TMS makes ratings of the weight of an object seen lifted noisier than in a sham condition.
source: For instance, disturbing the activity of the SI hand region with TMS makes ratings of the weight of an object seen lifted noisier than in a sham condition, suggesting that the region is necessary for transforming observed hand kinematics into an estimate of the forces that have been acting on the hand (Valchev et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Valchev et al., 2017.

claim: The SI hand region is necessary for transforming observed hand kinematics into an estimate of the forces that have been acting on the hand.
source: For instance, disturbing the activity of the SI hand region with TMS makes ratings of the weight of an object seen lifted noisier than in a sham condition, suggesting that the region is necessary for transforming observed hand kinematics into an estimate of the forces that have been acting on the hand (Valchev et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on cited research.

claim: A neural network including SI informs the participant on how intense the swat was on a given trial.
source: In this interpretation, a neural network including SI informs the participant on how intense the swat was on a given trial, and determines the ability of the participant to adjust the donation to the circumstances of a specific trial.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The mean donation could reflect trait differences in empathic concern and money attitude.
source: By contrast, the mean donation could reflect trait differences in empathic concern (measured by the Interpersonal Reactive Index [Davis, 1983]) and money attitude (Yamauchi and Templer, 1982) ('Supplemental analysis — Correlation with self-reported questionnaires').
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with reference to supplemental analysis.

claim: Activity in the hand region of SI that occurs while witnessing the bodily reactions of a victim to a painful stimulation is correlated with the willingness to help.
source: In summary, we provide evidence that activity in the hand region of SI that occurs while witnessing the bodily reactions of a victim to a painful stimulation is not only correlated with the willingness to help but significantly influences prosocial decision-making.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Activity in the hand region of SI significantly influences prosocial decision-making.
source: In summary, we provide evidence that activity in the hand region of SI that occurs while witnessing the bodily reactions of a victim to a painful stimulation is not only correlated with the willingness to help but significantly influences prosocial decision-making.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Altering SI activity influences the perception of other people's pain intensity.
source: Our data further constrain the mechanisms through which SI influences prosocial decision-making by showing that altering SI activity also influences the perception of other people's pain intensity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the HD-tDCS experimental data.

claim: The role of SI is to help transform the kinematics of affected body-parts into a perception of pain.
source: This suggests that the role of SI is to help us transform the kinematics of affected body-parts into a perception of pain, which is then a significant input to a decision-making process that occurs elsewhere in the brain.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation inferred from the combined experimental findings.

claim: If pain is not expressed through the affected body part but communicated through facial expressions, SI activity in the somatotopic representation of the initially affected body-part no longer seems to be a necessary input to decision-making.
source: If pain is not expressed through the affected body part but communicated through facial expressions, SI activity in the somatotopic representation of the initially affected body-part no longer seems to be a necessary input to this decision-making.
evidence: This is an interpretation inferred from the TMS experimental findings.

claim: Multiple networks, depending on the nature of the stimulus, can be recruited during the perception of the pain of others.
source: These neuromodulation findings support the notion derived from neuroimaging literature that multiple networks, depending on the nature of the stimulus, can be recruited during the perception of the pain of others (Keysers et al., 2010; Lamm et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion that integrates the current findings with cited literature.

claim: SI vicarious activations directly influence prosociality.
source: An empirical foundation for the intuitively attractive and often suggested causal links between the ability to represent what other people feel and prosocial actions is provided by the evidence that SI vicarious activations directly influence prosociality.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Racial biases modulate empathy.
source: Because previous studies reported that racial biases modulate empathy (Xu et al., 2009; Avenanti et al., 2010; Cikara et al., 2014) and our videos showed a Caucasian confederate, only Caucasian individuals were recruited.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and used as justification for participant selection.

claim: A total of 169 healthy, right-handed volunteers participated in the studies.
source: A total of 169 healthy, right-handed volunteers, with normal or corrected-to-normal vision, (mean age = 25 +/– 5 SD) were recruited for our studies (Table 1).
evidence: This is a demographic description of the participant sample.

claim: The hand area in the somatosensory cortex can be successfully targeted by positioning the coil 1–4 cm posterior to the motor hotspot.
source: A large body of evidence shows that the hand area in the somatosensory cortex can be successfully targeted by positioning the coil 1–4 cm posterior to the motor hotspot (Harris et al., 2002; Balslev et al., 2004; Merabet et al., 2004; Fiorio and Haggard, 2005; Tegenthoff et al., 2005; Bufalari et al., 2007; Azañón and Haggard, 2009; Jacquet and Avenanti, 2015; Valchev et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations and used as methodological justification.

claim: The high density 4 × 1 electrodes tDCS montage would be expected to have a facilitatory effect on the hand region of SI under the anode.
source: The high density 4 × 1 electrodes tDCS montage that we used would be expected to have a facilitatory effect on the hand region of SI under the anode (Figure 2D), and a weaker inhibitory effect on ventral SI, including the face representation, under one of the four return cathodes.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the known effects of the tDCS montage, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The high density 4 × 1 electrodes tDCS montage would be expected to have a weaker inhibitory effect on ventral SI under one of the four return cathodes.
source: The high density 4 × 1 electrodes tDCS montage that we used would be expected to have a facilitatory effect on the hand region of SI under the anode (Figure 2D), and a weaker inhibitory effect on ventral SI, including the face representation, under one of the four return cathodes.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the known effects of the tDCS montage, shown in Figure 2D.
